Four Touching Circles

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Four circles touch one another in a ring; move the dots and see what is always true about the four touching places.
How to play: Drag a circled dot, or focus it and press the arrow keys. Tick the box to see the flipped picture, or press Invert at E to turn two circles into straight lines.
Look for the math

Four round things in a ring, four places where neighbours meet. You would not expect those four places to sit on one circle — and yet, in the picture this applet can make, they always do. The catch is that the picture is a very special one.

The ring of four touches

The applet starts with two upright parallel lines through A and B. It then draws a circle through A and E that just touches the first line at A, and another through B and E that just touches the second line at B. Both circles pass through E, and they touch each other there: the centres are one radius apart in opposite directions. Parallel lines meet at the point at infinity, so the four contacts of the ring are A, E, B and that point — all on the line AB. A line counts as a circle through infinity here.

Flipping the picture in a circle

The pink circle has centre O and passes through R. Inversion in it sends a point P to the point on OP with distance R² / OP from O. It keeps angles, so touching curves still touch. Tick the box and you see the images: the two upright lines become two circles touching at O, the line AB becomes a circle through O, and the two drawn circles become two more circles (or lines, if you put O on them). Put O on E with the button and those two images really are parallel: the two circles touching at E have become straight lines, as the applet's own note says.

A, E, B on line AB  →  A′, E′, B′ on a circle through O.

That is the whole proof. The dashed circle you can see after ticking the box is the inverse of the line AB, so it passes through the centre of inversion O and through the three inverted contacts A′, E′, B′. In the page's version the inversion is centred at a touch, which makes those three images collinear; a line that does not go through the centre of inversion comes back as a circle through the centre. The logic test checks the circle through O, A′, E′, B′ at hundreds of random positions and at 998 positions of E along AB.

Where the page corrects itself

The page first states the theorem for any four circles touching in a ring, then adds a Remark: it is true only when the number of external touches is even (0, 2 or 4), and false for 1 or 3. This first applet always builds the even case — its two parallel lines cannot be modified into an odd one. Its sibling Four Touching Circles 3 lets you drag all four circles freely, and there the four contact points really do stop being concyclic. Our logic test builds 291 closed chains with chosen touch types and confirms the parity rule in every one. The unqualified opening claim is therefore false; the corrected version is what this page demonstrates.

About the original applet

The Java applet had one checkbox, "Inverted diagram", and circled points O and R for the inversion circle plus A, B and E for the chain; it drew the inverted images at all times and used the checkbox only to add the original construction lines. Here the checkbox swaps between the two views so they are easier to tell apart. One formula is refined: when O sits exactly on a circle, the applet drew an approximate tangent in place of the exact image line, while this page draws the true limit, at distance R²/(2r) from O and perpendicular to the line from O to the circle's centre. That is what makes the Invert at E button show truly parallel lines, as the page describes. All other formulas follow the applet's bytecode. The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra figure instead of the Java applet, so the applet embed was verified in a 2007 Wayback snapshot of the same address (it has code="FourTouchingCircles"). The homothety argument on the page is unchanged by this presentation.

Press Invert at E and watch the two image circles become parallel lines; then tick the box off to see the original ring again.
